lead: A helical gear has teeth cut on a slant, not parallel to the shaft. The slant makes contact begin at one end of the tooth and roll across the face, so the load is shared over a longer line. The gear runs quieter and carries more load than a spur gear of the same size. The same slant creates an axial thrust. That thrust changes the shaft and bearing design, and it is the main reason helical gears are not just better spur gears. They are common in vehicle and industrial gearboxes.
prereq: You need: Chapter 7.3 for the Lewis equation and Chapter 7.1 for involute profiles and gear nomenclature.

sections.h3: Helix angle and the two modules

blocks.text: A spur tooth meets its mate across the full face at once. A helical tooth is cut at a helix angle ψ to the shaft axis, so contact begins at one end of the face and travels across it. The contact line is longer and the load is shared more gradually. The result is quieter running, less impact and more load capacity at the same size. The price is an axial thrust that a spur gear does not have.

Two planes matter. The normal plane is perpendicular to the tooth; the transverse plane is perpendicular to the shaft. The standard cutter is defined in the normal plane, so the normal module mn is the standard value. The transverse module is mt = mn / cos ψ. Module is the pitch diameter per tooth, in millimetres. The transverse pitch is pt = π mt. The axial pitch, the distance between corresponding points of adjacent teeth along the shaft, is px = pt / tan ψ.

The pressure angle also changes with the plane. If φn is the normal pressure angle and φt is the transverse pressure angle, tan φn = tan φt cos ψ. Standard values are mn and φn; the designer calculates mt and φt for the transverse plane. Typical helix angles are 8° to 20°. Larger angles give smoother contact but larger thrust.

The normal plane cuts the pitch cylinder in an ellipse, not a true circle, so the tooth curvature in that plane is larger than the pitch radius. A spur gear with that curvature would have more teeth. That equivalent spur gear has the virtual, or formative, number of teeth zv = z / cos³ ψ, where z is the actual number of teeth and ψ is the helix angle. For ψ = 15° and z = 20, zv = 22.2, so the tooth behaves like a 22-tooth spur tooth. Some syllabi write β for the helix angle and call zv the formative number of teeth.

The Lewis form factor y is read for zv, not z. The modified Lewis equation for helical gears is σ = Ft / (Cv b π mn y). Here σ is the bending stress at the tooth root in N/mm², Ft is the tangential load at the pitch circle in N, b is the face width in mm, mn is the normal module in mm, y is the tooth form factor for zv, and Cv is the velocity factor from Chapter 7.3. The factor y comes from the standard tooth form and is about 0.1 for common tooth numbers; the π appears because y is defined through the circular pitch. Some tables list Y = πy instead, with values around 0.3 to 0.4; then use σ = Ft / (Cv b mn Y). Never mix a table of y with the form of the equation that expects Y. Use mn because the Lewis cantilever is taken on the normal tooth section. Using mt here overestimates the tooth thickness and gives an unsafe design.

Helical gears also have overlap. The transverse contact ratio εα is found as for a spur gear in the transverse plane. The overlap ratio is εβ = b sin ψ / (π mn). Total contact ratio is ε = εα + εβ. Overlap keeps more than one tooth in contact and smooths the drive. A total ratio above about 2 is common in quiet gearboxes.

sections.h3: Forces, thrust and hand of helix

blocks.text: The torque T on a gear gives the tangential force Ft = 2T / d = P / v. T is torque in N·mm, d is pitch diameter in mm, P is power in W and v is pitch line velocity in m/s; use consistent units. The diameter is d = mt z = mn z / cos ψ. The same Ft acts at the pitch circle.

The tooth also pushes radially and axially. The radial force is Fr = Ft tan φt = Ft tan φn / cos ψ. The axial thrust is Fa = Ft tan ψ. This thrust pushes the shaft along its axis, so the bearings must take it. A ball bearing with deep grooves takes little thrust; angular contact or tapered roller bearings are used. The shaft also bends under Ft and Fr and carries an axial load Fa. See Unit 5 for bearing selection.

Helices have a hand, right or left. Two parallel shafts need gears of opposite hand to mesh. The direction of thrust depends on hand and direction of rotation, so reverse rotation reverses Fa. A double helical gear, or herringbone gear, has two opposite helices on one body; the two thrusts cancel inside the gear and the bearings take almost no axial load. It costs more to make and needs space.

examples.question: A helical pair has mn = 3 mm, z1 = 20, z2 = 80, ψ = 15°, b = 45 mm, and transmits 11 kW at 1450 rpm. Find mt, d1, v, Ft, Fa and zv1.
steps: Helix angle ψ = 15°. Normal module mn = 3 mm. Transverse module mt = mn / cos ψ = 3 / cos 15° = 3 / 0.9659 = 3.106 mm.
Pitch diameter d1 = mt z1 = 3.106 × 20 = 62.12 mm, use 62.1 mm.
Pitch line velocity v = π d1 n1 / 60 with d1 in metres: v = π × 0.0621 × 1450 / 60 = 4.71 m/s.
Tangential force Ft = P / v = 11000 / 4.71 = 2335 N.
Axial thrust Fa = Ft tan ψ = 2335 × tan 15° = 2335 × 0.2679 = 626 N.
The radial force is Fr = Ft tan φn / cos ψ; φn is not given, so it is not calculated here.
examples.answer: The pair has mt = 3.106 mm, d1 = 62.1 mm, v = 4.71 m/s, Ft = 2335 N, Fa = 626 N and zv1 = 22.2.
examples.check:
import math
P = 11000.0
n = 1450.0
mn = 3.0
z1 = 20.0
psi = math.radians(15.0)
mt = mn / math.cos(psi)
d1 = round(mt * z1, 1)
v = round(math.pi * (d1 / 1000.0) * n / 60.0, 2)
Ft = round(P / v)
Fa = round(Ft * math.tan(psi))
zv1 = round(z1 / math.cos(psi)**3, 1)
print(round(mt, 3))
print(d1)
print(v)
print(Ft)
print(Fa)
print(zv1)

traps: Using mt in the modified Lewis equation. The Lewis section is normal, so use mn and y for zv.
Forgetting Fa = Ft tan ψ in shaft and bearing loads. The gear looks like a spur gear in side view but the axial thrust is real.
Using z instead of zv = z / cos³ ψ for the Lewis form factor, and using Fr = Ft tan φn without dividing by cos ψ.
Degree/radian slip and hand errors: tan ψ needs ψ in the calculator's unit; gears on parallel shafts need opposite hand.

quiz.q: Define helix angle ψ and normal module mn for a helical gear.
quiz.a: Helix angle ψ is the angle between the tooth trace and the shaft axis. Normal module mn is the module measured in the plane perpendicular to the tooth, and it is the standard cutter value.

quiz.q: Why is a helical gear quieter than a spur gear of the same size, and what new load appears?
quiz.a: Contact starts at one end of the helical tooth and moves across the face, so load is shared gradually over a longer line. The new load is axial thrust Fa = Ft tan ψ, which must be carried by the bearings.

quiz.q: A helical gear has mn = 4 mm, ψ = 20° and z = 25. Find mt, pitch diameter d and virtual teeth zv.
A helical gear transmits Ft = 3000 N with ψ = 18° and φn = 20°. Find the axial thrust Fa and radial force Fr.
quiz.a: Fa = Ft tan ψ = 3000 × tan 18° = 975 N. Fr = Ft tan φn / cos ψ = 3000 × tan 20° / cos 18° = 1148 N.

quiz.q: Explain why zv = z / cos³ ψ is used in the modified Lewis equation.
quiz.a: The normal plane cuts the pitch cylinder in an ellipse whose radius of curvature is r / cos² ψ. This makes the tooth behave like a spur gear with z / cos³ ψ teeth. The Lewis factor for that larger zv is larger, so the calculated stress is lower than using z alone.

quiz.q: Two helical gears on parallel shafts are both right hand. Will they mesh? What should be used instead?
quiz.a: Same hand on parallel shafts will not mesh; the teeth lean the same way and interfere. Use one right-hand and one left-hand gear. The two gears then have equal and opposite thrust, so each shaft needs a locating bearing (angular contact or tapered roller) to take its own thrust; the other bearing is left free to float.

quiz.q: Write the relation between normal pressure angle φn and transverse pressure angle φt.
quiz.a: tan φn = tan φt cos ψ, where ψ is the helix angle.

quiz.q: Why must axial thrust be included in shaft and bearing design?
quiz.a: Axial thrust adds a direct axial load to the shaft and a thrust load to the bearing. If it is left out, the bearing life and shaft stress are underestimated, and the bearing may be the wrong type.

beyond: Not for the exam. Helical gears are the default in electric-vehicle reducers and wind-turbine gearboxes because quiet high-speed operation matters. Design software adds profile and lead modification so contact stays away from tooth ends under load. Researchers study transmission error and mesh stiffness to predict whine. Search for helical gear transmission error, lead crowning and herringbone gearbox.
